# Would the green van hit the light-gray SUV if it drove straight ahead?

**Short answer: No. If the green van rolled straight forward along the direction
its front is pointing, it would not touch the light-gray SUV. The two vehicles
are pointing in roughly the same direction rather than at one another, and — this
is the decisive point — they are not in the same line at all: the SUV is standing
some 25–30 m nearer the camera than the van, so it lies off to the van's side
and slightly behind it, not in front of it. The van's forward path sweeps across
the scene at the van's own, much greater distance and clears the SUV comfortably.**

## Which two vehicles are meant

Everything of interest is in the bottom-left corner of the photograph, below and
to the left of the cathedral, in front of the row of yellow, green and cream
townhouses.

* The **light-gray SUV** is the silver Nissan Qashqai whose square tailgate, red
  tail-lights and white Estonian number plate `033 TJC` face towards the right of
  the frame. It is the right-hand car of a group of three parked cars (a dark
  sedan cut by the frame edge, a dark hatchback, then the silver SUV).
* The **green van** is the bright green one-box MPV (a Ford Galaxy/S-Max-shaped
  people carrier with roof rails) that appears immediately to the right of the
  SUV in the picture, beyond the bollards-and-chain and the give-way sign, in
  front of the cream-coloured building.

## Point 1 — Both vehicles face the same way: towards the left of the picture

Both cars are seen essentially in flank view, and both noses point to the **left**
of the frame, both tails to the **right**.

* The SUV shows us its **back end**: at its right-hand end we see the near-vertical
  tailgate, the rear screen, the tail-light cluster and the licence plate; the
  glasshouse tapers forwards to the windscreen, door mirror and bonnet at its
  left-hand end. So the SUV is aimed leftwards — away from the van.
* The green van is aimed the same way: its left-hand end is the low, forward-
  dropping bonnet running up into a steeply raked windscreen (the classic MPV
  front), while its right-hand end is the blunt, upright tail with a tail-light.

So the two are **roughly co-directional** — near-parallel and both facing left.
Neither is facing the other. Already this rules out a head-on geometry; the only
way a collision could happen is if the SUV happened to sit directly ahead of the
van on the van's own line of travel. It does not, for the reason below.

## Point 2 — They are at very different distances, which is what the image really shows

It is tempting to read the picture as "two cars parked nose-to-tail in one row,
van behind, SUV in front", because the SUV's rear corner overlaps the van's nose
in the image. That overlap is **not** evidence of a shared line. It is only
evidence of *occlusion order*: the SUV hides part of the van, so the SUV is the
**nearer** of the two. Measurement shows the gap is very large:

* **Apparent size.** The SUV's body measures about 168 px from roof to the ground
  at its tyres; the green van measures only about 107 px. Since a compact SUV and
  an MPV are of near-identical real height (an MPV is if anything the taller), an
  apparent-height ratio of roughly 1.6 means the van is roughly **1.5–1.7 times
  farther from the camera than the SUV**. This comparison is independent of the
  lens used.
* **Ground contact.** On a flat ground plane, the height in the image at which a
  vehicle's tyres meet the ground encodes its distance. The SUV's wheels touch
  down near image row 3003; the van's touch down near row 2945 — nearly 60 px
  higher up the frame, i.e. much closer to the horizon and therefore much farther
  away. The two cars parked alongside the SUV touch down at essentially the same
  rows as the SUV (~3003–3010), confirming they form one row at one distance and
  that the van is an outlier standing well beyond that row.
* **Scale cross-check.** The pedestrians confirm this. The person standing beside
  the SUV is drawn distinctly larger in the frame than the red-jacketed person
  standing out by the van, even though the latter is in front of the van rather
  than behind it.

Putting numbers on it with a reconstruction of the ground plane (horizon near row
2850, camera about 1.3 m above the pavement): the SUV sits roughly 45 m from the
camera and the van roughly 70–75 m — so the van is about **25–30 m deeper into
the scene**, past the junction, level with the cream "POST"-fronted building,
while the SUV is parked in the near row of cars on this side of it.

## Point 3 — Because the van is so much farther away, it is also farther LEFT in the real world

This is the step that overturns the naive reading. In the image the van appears
to the *right* of the SUV, which suggests it is behind the SUV in a shared line
running left. But image position mixes sideways offset with distance: a point's
sideways world offset is its image offset multiplied by its distance. The van's
image offset from the centre of the frame is about 0.8 times the SUV's, yet the
van is about 1.6 times farther away — 0.8 × 1.6 ≈ 1.3. In real-world terms the
van is therefore about 30 % **farther to the left** of the camera's axis than the
SUV is (roughly 25 m of lateral offset versus 18 m). It only looks like it is on
the SUV's right because things farther away are pulled towards the centre of the
picture.

So, taking a bird's-eye view of the scene with the camera at the bottom: the SUV
sits at about (18 m left, 45 m away) and the van at about (25 m left, 73 m away).
The straight line from the van to the SUV runs mostly **towards the camera** and
only slightly sideways.

## Point 4 — Put the orientation and the position together

The van's forward direction is "towards the left of the picture", which in the
bird's-eye view is a direction running roughly **across** the camera's line of
sight, keeping the van at about the same 70-odd metres of depth (it is seen in
near-full flank, so its axis is nearly perpendicular to the viewing direction; it
can be tilted a little away from or towards the camera, but not much).

The direction from the van to the SUV, by contrast, points mainly **back towards
the camera**. The angle between the van's heading and the bearing of the SUV is
therefore close to 90°, in fact slightly more than 90° — the SUV lies off the
van's near-side flank and marginally to its rear. The SUV's perpendicular
distance from the van's forward line is on the order of **25–30 m**.

Consequently, if the van moved straight ahead it would drive leftwards across the
top of the scene, keeping its distance from the camera, and pass a long way
beyond the SUV, which would be left behind it and off to the side. Even allowing
generously for measurement error in the van's heading — say ±20° — the SUV never
comes near the van's forward axis, because the SUV is displaced from it almost
perpendicularly, which is the least favourable direction for a collision.

## What would have to be true for a collision, and why it isn't

A nose-to-tail collision needs two things: the SUV must lie ahead of the van
along the van's own axis (not merely ahead of it in the picture), and the two
axes must be close to collinear rather than merely parallel. The first fails
because the SUV is 25–30 m nearer the camera — it is beside the van's path, not
on it. The second fails for the same reason: parallel-but-offset lines never
meet, and here the offset is many car-widths, not a few centimetres. The
overlapping of the SUV's rear corner and the van's nose in the photograph is a
projection artefact of the SUV being much closer to the lens, not a sign that
they share a lane.

**Conclusion: no collision. (1) Both vehicles face the same way, towards the left
of the frame, so they are not aimed at each other. (2) The SUV is about 25–30 m
nearer the camera than the van, as its much larger image size and much lower
ground contact both show. (3) Allowing for that depth difference, the van is
actually farther to the left in the real world than the SUV, so the SUV sits off
the van's near flank and slightly to its rear. (4) The van's straight-ahead path
runs across the scene at the van's own distance, missing the SUV by roughly the
whole 25–30 m depth gap between them.**

# Would the green van hit the light grey SUV?

**Short answer: No.** If the green van drove straight ahead in the direction its nose points, it would not collide with the light grey SUV. It would drive off to the left along its own roadway and pass well behind the SUV, missing it by many metres. The two vehicles only appear to be nose-to-tail because of the flat 2-D projection of the photograph; in real space they are on different roadways at very different distances from the camera, and the SUV lies outside the van's line of travel.

## 1. The two vehicles and which way each one faces

**The green van** is the dark-green MPV (people-carrier) parked in the background at the lower-left of the photo, in front of the yellow building with the white columned portico and the "POST" sign. It stands behind a traffic-sign post on a stone base, behind a low bollard-and-chain fence, and next to a cast-iron lamp post. Its sloping bonnet and raked windscreen are at its **left** end and its upright tailgate is at its **right** end (part of the tail is hidden by the lamp-post base). So the van faces **left** in the frame. We see its full flank, its wheels look almost perfectly round, and its roof and window line stay level from end to end; this means the van is standing almost broadside to the camera, i.e. its long axis runs roughly parallel to the picture plane (left–right across the scene), not toward or away from the viewer.

**The light grey SUV** is the silver Nissan Qashqai (registration 033 TJC) that stands nearer the camera in the row of three cars at the left edge of the cobbled square (dark car, grey sedan, then the SUV). Its tailgate, rear number plate and tail-lights are turned toward the viewer, its flank recedes to the left, and its wheels appear as narrow ellipses because they are strongly foreshortened. That means the SUV is parked **diagonally**: its nose points up-and-left in the frame, i.e. away from the camera and to the left, at roughly 40–50° to the picture plane, and its rear is the part of it closest to the camera. In other words the SUV is *not* parallel to the van: the van points straight left, the SUV points diagonally away.

## 2. Where the two vehicles actually are

In the flat picture the van's nose seems to touch the SUV's rear bumper, so at a glance it looks as if the van is parked right behind the SUV in the same line. That is an overlap along the camera's line of sight, not real adjacency, and three independent depth cues prove it:

* **Occlusion.** The SUV's rear-left corner (its tail-light and rear bumper) is drawn *over* the van's front bumper and the lower part of the van's front wheel and hides them. The object doing the hiding is the nearer one, so the SUV is in front and the van is behind it, farther from the camera.
* **Ground line.** The van's tyres touch the ground noticeably higher in the frame (about 50 pixels in the full-resolution image) than the SUV's tyres. In a level street scene, a ground contact point higher in the frame is farther from the camera.
* **Apparent size.** The van is a full-size MPV, taller and longer than a Qashqai, yet it appears only about 60 % of the SUV's size in the picture (roof-to-ground roughly 100 px versus roughly 165 px; wheel rims roughly 30 px versus roughly 50 px). Something bigger that looks smaller must be much farther away. The scale ratio implies the van stands roughly one and a half times as far from the camera as the SUV, i.e. on the order of 10–25 m deeper into the scene – several car lengths – on the far side of the kerb, sign post, chain fence and lamp post that separate its roadway from the edge of the square where the SUV is parked.

There is a further perspective consequence. Both vehicles are far to the left of the picture centre, so the sight-line to them runs leftward as it goes deeper. Two objects that overlap in the picture but differ in depth are therefore also displaced sideways in real space: the deeper one (the van) is farther to the left. In plan view the van's nose is already roughly level with, or even slightly beyond, the SUV's front end in the direction the van points. The van is not "behind" the SUV at all in real space; it is behind-and-beyond it, off to the far side.

## 3. Putting orientation and position together

The van's straight-line path is a line running to the left, parallel (to within about 10–15°) to the picture plane, at the van's own large depth. The SUV occupies a slanted footprint at a much shallower depth: its rear is the closest point to the camera and even its nose – its deepest point, because it is turned away from the viewer – is still many metres short of the van's line. So:

* The van's path never reaches the SUV's depth: the SUV is entirely between the camera and the van's line of travel, with a gap of several car lengths.
* The van's path never reaches the SUV's sideways position either: the van is already level with or past the SUV's front end, and driving forward carries it further left, *away* from the SUV. To touch the SUV the van would have to move both backward (to the right) and toward the camera at the same time, which straight forward motion cannot do.
* Even allowing for the van being angled a few degrees toward the camera (a sliver of its sunlit front face is visible), it would have to travel far more than 100 m sideways before its depth changed enough to matter, and by then it would be far to the left of the SUV anyway.

The SUV's own orientation reinforces the miss. Because the SUV is turned diagonally with its tail toward the viewer, its body runs from near-right (rear) to far-left (front). The van's line, lying at a constant and much greater depth, never crosses that diagonal strip. A collision would require one of two different configurations that are not present: either the SUV standing broadside on the same far roadway directly to the van's left, or the van standing in the same diagonal parking row immediately behind the SUV and pointing the same diagonal direction, with its nose aimed at the SUV's tailgate.

## Conclusion

No. The green van faces left and is standing broadside to the camera on a roadway well behind the row of parked cars; the light grey SUV is parked diagonally, nose away from the viewer, in the nearer row, closer to the camera and no farther left than the van's nose. Driving straight ahead, the van would run leftward along the far roadway and pass behind the SUV (and the rest of that parked row) with a clearance of many metres. The apparent nose-to-tail contact in the photograph is a depth illusion created by two vehicles at very different distances lining up along the same sight-line.
